body.text:
I brushed a second dog out of my first dog. He had been wearing it since March.

I need to show you what came off of my golden retriever in one ten-minute session, and then I need to explain what it actually was, because the explanation is the part that stopped being funny.

My name is Aaron. I'm 38. Murphy is my golden, four years old, brushed twice a week his whole life, or so I sincerely believed.

Two Sundays ago I used a real deshedding tool on him for the first time. Ten minutes on the patio. And when I was done, there was a pile of fur on the ground next to my dog that was, and I am not exaggerating because I took photos with my shoe in them for scale, roughly the size of a small spaniel.

A second dog. Sitting on my patio. Extracted from my first dog.

My wife came outside, looked at the pile, looked at Murphy, looked back at the pile, and said, "Where was he keeping all of that?"

That question is this entire post. Because I found out where he was keeping it, and it changed how I think about brushing, shedding, and every tumbleweed of fur I've chased across my kitchen for four years.

Here's where he was keeping it.

A golden's coat is two coats. The outer guard hairs, the shiny gold everyone pets. And underneath, a thick soft undercoat, his insulation. That undercoat is constantly dying and regrowing, and the dead fur doesn't just fall out. Most of it can't get out. It's trapped under the guard hairs, packed in layer after layer, month after month.

The spring shed I thought had "ended" in April? It never ended. It just got stuck. Murphy had been carrying his entire spring coat, dead, compressed against his skin, through May, June, and the hottest July on record.

He wasn't wearing a coat. He was wearing a coat with a dead coat trapped inside it.

And once I understood that, three mysteries in my house solved themselves in about thirty seconds.

Mystery one: why the shedding never stops. The tumbleweeds aren't him shedding fresh fur. They're the trapped reservoir leaking out, a little at a time, forever. You cannot vacuum your way ahead of a reservoir. I have tried. I own the vacuum receipts.

Mystery two: why my "brushed twice a week" dog produced a spaniel-sized pile. My pet store brush grooms the surface coat. It has never once reached the reservoir. Four years of brushing the outside of a full container.

Mystery three, and this is the one that got me: why Murphy, a dog with a cooling mat he loves, still spent afternoons flat on the tile looking defeated. He was insulated. Wrapped in a dead layer that blocks airflow to his skin and holds his own warmth and dander against him. My dog was wearing a blanket in July, sewn shut, and no amount of AC touches a blanket you can't take off.

So, the tool, because everyone asks and I'd rather tell you than have you buy the wrong thing like I nearly did.

It's called the GroomPro. It's the same blade-style comb groomers use on the table, a real groomer blade in a consumer handle, which reaches through the guard hairs and pulls out the dead undercoat instead of skating over it. Two things made it the pick. It's built nick-free, no pressure needed, and Murphy, a dog who used to negotiate every brushing like a hostage situation, went boneless for it by minute three, because nothing pulls. And the stainless comb pops off and replaces in seconds, so the thing is built to be the last brush I buy rather than this year's brush.

$34. Works on dogs and cats, short coats through double coats like Murphy's. 30-day money-back guarantee, which given what you're about to pull out of your own dog is the safest bet in pet products.

The after-effects, two weeks in, in ascending order of how much they shocked me:

The tumbleweeds are down to almost nothing, because the reservoir is empty and staying empty on a ten-minute weekly schedule.

Murphy's coat looks absurd. Lighter, lifted, shinier, moving in the breeze like a shampoo commercial, because it's finally just the living coat.

And the tile time dropped. He's back on his cooling mat and the couch and generally circulating like a dog instead of lying flat like a rug, because the blanket is off. I did not expect a brush to change where my dog lies in the afternoon. The blanket explanation is the only one that fits.

Here's what I want you to actually do, and it's free.

Part the fur on your dog's back right now, anywhere, down to the skin. If you see a dense woolly felt-like layer packed down there, grey or dull against the bright topcoat, congratulations, you've located the second dog. He's been wearing it since spring. It sheds into your house on a payment plan, it itches, and in this heat it insulates, and no surface brush you own has ever touched it.

Ten minutes. That's what it takes to take the blanket off.

The GroomPro is linked below. Bring a bag for the pile. You're going to want photos.

P.S. The pile photo is mandatory, I don't make the rules. Every person who uses a real deshedding tool for the first time takes the same picture, the pile next to the dog, the dog looking slim and confused, and posts it with some version of "WHERE WAS HE KEEPING THIS." Tag someone with a golden, a Lab, or a husky when you post yours. That photo does more good than this whole ad. Linked below.

P.P.S. For the short-coat crowd about to scroll past: my brother has a Frenchie and borrowed mine as a joke. The joke produced a softball-sized pile off a dog with quote unquote no undercoat, and he ordered his own from my kitchen. Shedding starts in the layer you can't see on every coat length. The comb doesn't care how smug the breed is. Linked below.

body.text:
Do not shave your dog this summer. My groomer made me promise to post this before another July.

I'm keeping the promise, and I'm qualified to keep it, because I am the before AND the after of this story. I shaved one golden retriever for years out of love. I have never shaved the second one, and the difference taught me everything.

My name is Carmen. I'm 48. And every July, right about now, thousands of loving owners look at a panting double-coated dog, feel that ache in their chest, and book the appointment I used to book. The shave-down. The summer cut. The mercy haircut.

I need to walk you through why that mercy is aimed backwards, the way my groomer walked me through it, because once you see how the coat actually works, you cannot unsee it.

My first golden was Cooper. Every May, I had him shaved nearly to the skin, and I want you to understand my logic, because it's your logic. I wear a coat in winter and take it off in summer. He wears a coat. Therefore.

Here's what I actually observed across those summers, and explained away every single time. Cooper still panted, honestly as much as ever. He started getting hot spots. He sunburned once, pink skin through stubble, which baffled me. And around year four, his coat started coming back wrong. Patchy. Wooly. Duller each time. The groomer at the chain place shrugged and clipped it again.

Cooper lived a good long life and I'd give anything for one more July of him, shaved or not. But when Ginger came along, dark red and gorgeous, I called a new groomer in June and asked for the summer cut.

And she said no.

She actually said, "I won't do that to a double-coated dog, but come in anyway and I'll show you what I'll do instead." There's a handwritten sign at her counter, taped next to the register: "We do not shave double-coated breeds. Ask us why." So I asked. Here's why, as close to her words as I can get them.

A double coat is not a jacket. It's a system with two parts doing two jobs. The soft undercoat underneath is insulation, and insulation works in both directions. It slows heat coming in just like it slows heat going out. It's the same reason a cooler keeps things cold in a hot car. And the outer guard hairs are the armor: they block sun off the skin and let air move through the gaps.

When that system is healthy, with air circulating through it, it's part of how the dog manages summer. When you shave it, you take away the sun armor and the thermal buffer at the same time. Pink skin meets July sun directly. And here's the cruelest part: it grows back wrong. The undercoat regrows faster than the guard hairs, so what returns is often a dense wooly layer with thin armor over it, sometimes patchy, sometimes permanently changed. Which explained Cooper's fourth-year coat in one sentence, eight years too late.

Then she said the thing that made me get it, the thing I promised to repeat.

"People shave because the coat feels like the problem. The coat is not the problem. The dead fur PACKED INSIDE the coat is the problem. It's like your attic is stuffed to the rafters, so the whole house is stuffy, and your solution is to rip the roof off. Don't demolish the house. Clean out the attic."

The dead undercoat. The fur that's already shed but never made it out, trapped under the guard hairs in a compressed layer, blocking exactly the airflow the system depends on, holding warmth and dander right against the skin. That's the stuffiness. That's the panting-on-the-bed misery. That's what people are actually trying to shave off, one layer too deep.

The fix is removal of the dead layer only, and the system stays intact. She did it on her table that day with a deshedding blade, and the cloud of grey dead wool that came off Ginger, off a dog I brushed regularly with a normal brush, filled a grocery bag. The living coat stayed. The armor stayed. The insulation stayed. Only the attic junk left.

For home, between visits, she told me exactly what to get: a groomer-blade deshedding tool, and she was specific that it be a nick-free one that needs no pressure, because pressure is how home grooming goes wrong. The one that matched her spec is the GroomPro, the same blade style as her table tool in a $34 handle, with a stainless comb that quick-releases and replaces so it stays effective for years. Ten minutes, once or twice a week in shedding season. Ginger gets hers on the porch on Sundays, and she leans into it, because removing an itchy dead layer apparently feels as good as it sounds.

body.text:
My son's allergist asked one question that kept our dog in this family. It wasn't about the dog.

I need to tell this story carefully, because the version of me from last spring is reading this right now with a lump in her throat, and I know exactly which post she has sitting in her drafts.

My name is Priya. I'm 39. Eli is seven. Toby is our yellow Lab, and Eli has loved him since before Eli could say his name, back when he was just "Doh."

Last spring, Eli's allergies got worse. The stuffiness that never cleared, the itchy eyes, the nighttime cough. We did the responsible things, and the testing came back with the result I had been quietly dreading for a year.

Dog dander. Among other things, but there it was, on paper, with a number next to it.

If you have never sat in a paper-gown room while a doctor's words quietly rearrange your family, I hope you never do. Nobody said the word out loud in that appointment. They didn't have to. The word rode home in the car with us anyway, sitting between the booster seat and the dog hair on the upholstery.

Rehome.

I'm going to be honest about the next part because I promised myself I would.

Three nights later, at 1 AM, I sat in the dark and typed the post. "Rehoming our sweet boy. Toby is 5, house-trained, wonderful with kids..." I got as far as choosing the photos. Toby asleep at the foot of Eli's bed in every single one, which is when I stopped being able to see the screen, and I put the phone face down, and I did not post it.

I never posted it. Here's what happened instead.

At the follow-up, the allergist walked us through management before anything drastic, and she was systematic about it in a way I'll be grateful for forever. HEPA filters, yes. Bedroom as a dog-free zone, hard but yes. Washing hands after petting, soft furnishings, all of it. And then she looked up from the checklist and asked:

"What are you brushing him with, and how often?"

I almost laughed. My son is wheezing and we're discussing my brush?

But she was completely serious, and what she explained next is the reason Toby is asleep in the hallway outside Eli's door as I type this.

The allergen isn't the hair. It's the dander, the microscopic skin particles, and proteins that ride on the hair. And in a shedding dog, the biggest reservoir of dander in your entire home is not the couch or the carpet. It's the layer of dead undercoat packed inside the dog's own coat, loaded with dander, releasing into the house continuously, hair by hair, all day, every day. You vacuum the carpet, and the reservoir restocks the carpet by dinnertime.

"Most families fight the allergen everywhere it lands," she said. "You'll do better fighting it where it lives. Get the dead undercoat out of the dog, outdoors, on a schedule, before it distributes itself through your house. It won't cure anything. It shrinks the source. Combined with everything else on this list, shrinking the source is often what makes the difference between manageable and not."

Not a cure. A shrink. I want to be precise about that the way she was, because I've seen the miracle-cure posts and I refuse to write one. Eli still has his treatment. The HEPA filters still run. The bedroom is still dog-free, which Toby protests nightly from the hallway with theatrical sighs.

But the brush question changed our house, so here is what we do.

Every Sunday, outside on the patio, Toby gets ten minutes with a GroomPro. It's a groomer-blade deshedding tool, the kind that reaches through the topcoat and extracts the dead, dander-loaded undercoat itself, instead of skimming the surface like the brush we'd owned for years, which, per the allergist, had been rearranging the outside of the reservoir. It's nick-free and takes no pressure, so Toby thinks it's a spa appointment, and the extraction happens where she told us it should: outdoors, into the bag, straight into the bin. Not through my son's air first.

The first session filled a produce bag. A produce bag of exactly the material we'd been living inside of.

Where we are now, four months in, with all credit shared across the entire plan: the ambient hair in the house has collapsed. The wipe-down cloths come away lighter. Eli's flare-ups have eased to where his doctor is pleased at check-ins, and I will not claim more than that, because his allergist earned my trust by being exact and I intend to keep the habit.

And the draft is deleted. Not saved for later. Deleted.

Here is why I'm posting this, one year almost to the week from that paper-gown room.

Somewhere tonight there's a parent with the post half-typed and the photos chosen, sitting in the dark doing the math between two kinds of heartbreak. I can't promise you our outcome, and neither can anyone else, your allergist is the only one who knows your child's case. But before the post goes up, ask them the management question. Ask specifically about the coat, the dead undercoat, the source. Make them walk you through the whole checklist first.

Because the fix for us wasn't choosing between the boy and the dog. It was a checklist, a doctor who asked about my brush, and ten minutes on the patio every Sunday.

The tool is the GroomPro. $34, dogs and cats, gentle enough that ours campaigns for it, 30-day money-back guarantee. It is not medicine, and I'll say it as many times as it takes. It's housekeeping at the source. In this house, housekeeping at the source is part of why everyone still lives here.

It's linked below. Toby says hi from the hallway.

P.S. If you're the parent with the draft: screenshot the checklist that saved us and bring it to your appointment. HEPA in the main rooms and bedroom. Dog-free sleeping room. Hard floors where possible, hot-wash soft things. Hands washed after big cuddle sessions. And weekly deshedding, outdoors, at the source, with a tool that actually reaches the undercoat. Then let the doctor tailor it. The draft can wait one appointment. Ours never got posted. Linked below.

P.P.S. To everyone about to comment that severe allergies sometimes leave families no choice: you're right, and those families deserve zero judgment, and this post is not for or about them. It's for the family that was told "the dander" and heard "the dog," and never got asked the brush question. It took one appointment to change our answer. Ask it. Linked below.

He is a big fluffy boy, so I was certain this was a hair problem. When he got backed up, I blamed his coat.

So I brushed him every day. I paid for the lion cut twice a shedding season. And every time, the constipation eased for a couple of weeks, then came back the moment his fur grew out.

I had half of it right. The hair really was part of it.

What I did not understand is why the hair jammed at all, when other cats swallow just as much and pass it fine. Read this if you have a long-haired cat who keeps backing up.

The brushing is not going to fix this on its own.

Neither is the next lion cut.

Not the hairball paste. Not the hairball food. Not the fountain the pet store swore by.

I know, because I did all of it. For over a year. My cat still ended up on an emergency table with a colon packed solid.

Read this whole thing. Every word. Because the missing half is in here. And it is not another haircut.

My name is Martha Bennett. I am 54.

I live in Burlington, Vermont with my husband Tom and a seal-point Ragdoll named Moose.

Moose is nine. Fourteen pounds of fur and blue eyes.

He is the softest, floppiest, most patient animal I have ever known. You can carry him like a baby and he goes limp and purrs.

Before I tell you the story, I want to say one thing up front. Because I would have wanted to hear it first.

The thing that finally fixed Moose was not a drug. It was not another laxative I had to keep increasing. It was one thing his body is supposed to have plenty of and did not.

It is safe to give every day. There is nothing in it to overdose on. Anything his body does not use, he just pees out.

I gave it to him alongside everything his vet already had him on. It did not fight with any of it.

I will get to what it is. But you need the story first, or the answer will sound too simple to believe.

Because Moose is long-haired. And for most of his life I was sure that fact was the whole story with his gut.

Moose has always been a constipation cat.

It started around age six. Slow trips to the box. Squatting. Nothing. Then a hard little pellet, like a dry marble, a day later.

He is long-haired. So I did the math the way any long-hair owner does.

Long coat. Grooms himself all day. Swallows fur constantly. The fur is backing him up.

That made sense to me. It still makes sense to me. Because part of it is true.

So I treated it like a hair problem. Every product I bought was a hair product.

I brushed him every single day. A slicker brush, then a metal comb, then a deshedding tool. I filled a grocery bag with his fur every week in shedding season.

I bought the hairball control food. The one with the extra fiber, in the green bag.

I bought Laxatone. The brown malt gel. Moose hated it. I had to smear it on his front paw so he would lick it off. When it ran out I bought the Nutri-Vet paste. Same idea.

And twice a year, in spring and fall, I paid seventy dollars to have him shaved into a lion cut.

And here is the thing. It worked. Sort of.

Every single time Moose got his lion cut, the constipation stopped. For a couple of weeks he pooped like a normal cat.

Then his coat grew back. And the straining came right back with it.

I said this to my sister once. It is so strange, I told her. Right after his haircut the constipation stops. When the hair grows out, it starts again.

I thought that proved my theory. Coat length and constipation moved together. Case closed. It was the hair.

I was half right. And being half right almost killed my cat.

Because I had the hair part. I did not have the other part. And nobody in my life had the other part either.

Let me tell you what happened last October.

Coat-blowing season hit hard.

Moose stopped going at all.

Two days. Three. He would go in the box, squat, strain, and come out with nothing. He stopped eating. He hid under the bed, which he never does.

On the third day I felt his belly. It was hard as a rock.

I drove him to the emergency vet at nine at night.

They took an x-ray. Ninety dollars.

The vet turned the screen toward me.

Moose's colon was packed solid, end to end. A dense, dark mass. She pointed to the texture of it.

See how it looks almost stringy in places, she said. That is fur. Long-haired cats do this. The hair mats into the stool and the whole thing dries into a brick.

So I was right. It was the hair.

They kept him overnight. They sedated him and did a manual disimpaction. Fluids under the skin. An enema.

That was six hundred and forty dollars.

I want to be clear about one thing. That part was the vet's job. When a cat is blocked up like that, you need a vet, that night. No supplement fixes an emergency. I am grateful they were open.

But then the vet said the part that scared me.

This is his second bad episode this year, she said. If it keeps happening, we start talking about megacolon. And the treatment for advanced megacolon can be surgery. A subtotal colectomy. We remove most of the colon.

Three thousand dollars. To take out my cat's colon.

She was kind about it. She was not wrong to raise it. But I drove home shaking.

That night I could not sleep.

I had done everything. The brushing. The lion cuts. The paste. The special food. And my cat still nearly died with a colon full of dried hair.

I opened my laptop at two in the morning.

I did not search cat constipation. I had read every page of that a hundred times. Pumpkin, water, fiber, I knew all of it.

I searched something different. I searched why long haired cats get so constipated and how to actually stop it.

That is when the forums took a turn I did not expect.

Post after post from long-hair owners. Ragdolls. Maine Coons. Big fluffy rescues. The exact same story. The lion cut that helps for two weeks. The paste the cat spits out. The vet threatening colon surgery.

And under those posts, over and over, one word I had never once connected to constipation.

Taurine.

Not for the heart. Not for the eyes. That is all I had ever heard taurine was for.

For water. For hydration. For moving a dry gut.

One woman wrote that her long-haired cat passed a giant hairball two days after she started it, then went back to normal, and she never looked back.

I ordered the first taurine I could find on Amazon that same night.

Some brand in a white tub. Twelve ninety-nine. Prime shipping.

I started mixing a scoop into Moose's wet food the day it arrived.

And I waited.

Three weeks went by.

A little better, maybe. Fewer misses at the box. But he was still straining. Still passing hard little pellets. Still nothing like a normal cat.

I started to think the internet had sold me another story. That taurine was just the new pumpkin.

I almost stopped.

Then his lion cut appointment came up. And that is where everything actually changed.

The groomer I had used for years had retired. There was someone new doing the cat grooming now. An older woman named Marlene.

She was calm with Moose in a way that surprised me. He usually hates the shave. With her he just melted.

While she worked, she asked how his year had been. I told her. The blockage. The emergency vet. The colectomy talk.

She stopped the clippers.

I did twenty-one years as a technician on an internal medicine service before I did this, she said. Mostly feline. I have seen more impacted long-haired cats than I can count.

Then she said the thing that rearranged my whole head.

You are not wrong about the hair. Long coats absolutely make this worse. But the hair is only half of it. And it is the half everybody stops at.

I asked her what the other half was.

Let me ask you something first, she said. Two cats swallow the same amount of hair. Why does one brick up, and one passes it just fine?

I did not have an answer.

Water, she said. Whether the gut is wet enough to move the hair along. That is the whole difference. And most cats are drier on the inside than anyone realizes.

Then she explained something I had never heard in my life.

Cats did not evolve to drink water.

They came from desert animals. Their ancestors got almost all their water from the bodies of the prey they ate.

To survive on so little, their cells rely on things called osmolytes.

Osmolytes are tiny water magnets inside the cells. They pull moisture in and lock it there.

Taurine, she said, is one of the biggest osmolytes in a cat's whole body.

Without enough taurine, the cells physically cannot hold water.

The cat gets dehydrated on the inside. Not the outside. The inside. The blood. The tissue. The gut wall.

Even if he drinks from a fountain. Even if he eats nothing but wet food.

The water goes in. He just cannot hold it. It passes straight through.

And here is what that does to the colon, Marlene said.

The colon's whole job is to pull water back out of the stool before it leaves the body.

When the body is short on water on the inside, the colon panics. It pulls back even harder. It wrings the stool bone dry.

Dry, hard, pellet stool. The kind I had been scooping for three years.

Now, she said, add a long coat to that.

In a hydrated cat, swallowed hair rides along in soft, moist stool and passes without anyone noticing.

In a dried-out gut, that same hair has nothing to carry it. It mats into the hard, dry stool. It knits the whole thing into a brick.

The hair is the rebar. The dryness is the concrete.

I sat there on that grooming stool and felt the floor drop.

That, Marlene said, is why the lion cut helps for two weeks and then quits. You take away some of the hair, so there is less to jam. But you never touched the dryness. So the second his coat grows back, the same dry gut bricks up around it again.

The haircut experiment I had been so proud of. She had just explained both halves of it.

The hair was real. But the hair only ever jammed because his gut was too dry to move it.

I asked her the question I already dreaded.

Then why did my vet never say any of this?

She did not blame him.

Because taurine deficiency is not on a standard panel, she said. There is no blood test they run for it. There is no prescription for it, because it is just an amino acid you can buy off a shelf. There is no money in it for anyone. So it sits outside the whole system. Your vet is not hiding it. It is just not on the map they are handed.

She said the disimpaction was the right call. The emergency care was the right call.

The vet handles the crisis, she said. This handles why the crisis keeps coming back. You do both. You do not pick one.

Then I told her about the Amazon taurine I had been giving Moose for three weeks.

I pulled the tub up on my phone and showed her.

She shook her head before I even finished.

I have had these tested, she said. Not this exact one, but ten just like it.

Most of the cheap ones test around a hundred and ninety four milligrams a scoop when the label claims five hundred.

And the form they use is barely absorbed. Around twenty eight percent.

So your cat is actually getting somewhere near fifty four milligrams, she said. A cat Moose's size, fourteen pounds, needs at least two hundred to move anything. You have been giving him almost nothing.

Three weeks of almost nothing. That was why he had barely improved.

And some of these, she said, come back from the lab with zero measurable taurine. Just filler in a nice tub.

I asked her what she used.

She wrote one name on the back of my receipt.

KittySupps.

It is what the specialists I still know actually reach for now, she said. Every batch third-party tested. Five hundred and three milligrams of real taurine a scoop. The label says five hundred. It runs a little over.

Ninety five to ninety eight percent absorbed, she said. Free-form, pharmaceutical grade, which means it does not need the whole bile process to get in. It goes straight into the bloodstream.

Completely tasteless. One scoop into the wet food. Moose would never know it was there.

Then she said the part that mattered most to me after the year I had.

It is an amino acid, not a drug, she said. It is water soluble. You cannot overdose him. Anything his body does not use, he pees out. No toxicity. No side effects. And it runs right alongside his lactulose, or his MiraLAX, or a kidney or thyroid medication, without any conflict.

About twenty dollars for a thirty day supply.

I ordered it in the parking lot before I even started the car.

I started Moose on it that night. One scoop in his wet food. He ate it like it was not there.

Week one. Not much. Still straining. I told myself to be patient.

Week two. The pellets got a little bigger. A little less dry.

Week three. He went in the box and produced like a normal cat for the first time in longer than I could remember. I actually called Tom in to look.

Week four. Soft belly when I picked him up. No more squatting for five minutes with nothing.

Week six. This is the part I still can hardly believe. Moose passed a huge amount of matted hair. All at once. And it kept moving through, easily, over the next few days.

The hair was not the enemy. The hair had always needed a wet gut to leave. Now it had one.

His coat is still long. He still swallows fur all day. I still brush him. I never stopped the brushing.

But the constipation did not come back when his coat grew out this time.

For the first time in years, the coat grew back and nothing bricked up.

I took him to his regular vet in the spring for a check.

His belly was soft. No sign of the impaction cycle. No colectomy conversation.

I told the vet it was taurine. There was a pause. Then he said, well, whatever you are doing, keep doing it.

That is the part I want you to hear. Keep doing it.

This is not a cure. I did not fix Moose once and walk away.

He gets his scoop every single day. He will get it every day for the rest of his life. The day I stop, his cells start drying out again, and the whole thing comes back.

It is a daily thing. Like brushing him. Except this one keeps him off the surgery table.

That was almost a year ago now. Moose is nine and a half. He plays. He flops. He poops like a normal cat.

And I have not paid for another emergency disimpaction since.

If you have a long-haired cat, and you have been fighting the constipation the way I did, I need you to hear this.

You were not wrong about the hair. The hair is real. Do not let anyone tell you it is all in your head.

But the hair is only half. And the half you were never told is the half that actually keeps him blocked.

I have read a hundred posts from people writing the exact words I used to write.

My long haired boy constantly has hairball issues.

A lot of his problems I think are caused by digested hair. Getting him shaved is the biggest help.

Right after she gets a haircut the constipation stops. When it grows out, it starts back up.

All three of mine end up backed up during coat-blowing season.

That was me. Every one of those was me.

You are not failing him. The brushing is not the wrong thing. It is just not the whole thing.

The reason the hair jams is that his gut is too dry to move it. And no lion cut, no paste, no amount of brushing fixes the dryness.

Taurine does. It puts the water back where the hair needs it.

One scoop of KittySupps in his wet food. Once a day. Tasteless. He will not know.
